---
title: "Choosing a criterion"
description: "Which training set criteria exist, which ones TSDFGS has, and what recent comparisons found."
---

A training set criterion is a number computed from genotypes alone that predicts how well a model trained on the chosen individuals will predict the others. The search then looks for the training set that optimizes it. This page lists the criteria in the literature, says which are in TSDFGS, and summarizes recent comparisons. The list is not complete; it covers the work we read in full or by abstract (see the references).

## Targeted and untargeted

* **Targeted**: the individuals to predict (the test set) are genotyped when the training set is chosen. The criterion compares the training set with the test set.
* **Untargeted**: only the candidate pool is known. The candidates left out of the training set act as the test set.

In a benchmark on seven data sets of six species, targeted optimization beat untargeted optimization, with the largest gap at low heritability (Fernández-González et al., 2023). Akdemir et al. (2019) reached the same conclusion.

## Criteria in TSDFGS

| Criterion | Idea | Direction | Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| **r-score** | Closed form of the Pearson correlation between predicted and observed values in the test set, for ridge regression (Ou & Liao, 2019) | larger | `r_score()` |
| **CD** | Coefficient of determination of the predictions, in the PC ridge form (Laloë et al., 1996) | larger | `cd_score()` |
| **PEV** | Prediction error variance (Akdemir et al., 2015) | smaller | `pev_score()` |

`optTrain(method = )` takes `"rScore"`, `"CD"`, or `"PEV"`.

The CD and PEV of TSDFGS are computed on the PCs with a ridge penalty. They are not the mixed-model CDmean and PEVmean of Rincent et al. (2012), which use a relationship matrix and a variance ratio; the packages STPGA and TrainSel implement those.

## Other criteria in the literature

These are not in TSDFGS v3.0-alpha.

| Criterion | Idea | Source |
|---|---|---|
| CDmean, PEVmean | Mean reliability (CD) or prediction error variance of the contrasts between each candidate and the population mean, from a relationship-matrix mixed model | Rincent et al. (2012); Akdemir et al. (2015) |
| Stratified CDmean | CDmean within sub-populations | Isidro et al. (2015) |
| Uniform coverage | Sample the genetic (PC) space uniformly, optionally within strata | Bustos-Korts et al. (2016) |
| Minimum average relationship | Choose a training set with the lowest mean relationship among its members (the best untargeted criterion in a seven-data-set benchmark) | Fernández-González et al. (2023) |
| CDmean(v2), MSPE-ridge, and genomic-variation rankings | Criteria aimed at finding the top genotypes, not at the mean accuracy; CDmean(v2) equals CDmean but is cheaper to compute | Chen et al. (2024) |
| Multi-environment and multi-trait criteria | CD or PEV on genotype-by-environment (-by-trait) kernels | Gevartosky et al. (2021); Liu & Liao (2026) |
| Diversity and core-set metrics | Distances between accessions, allelic richness | De Beukelaer et al. (2018) |
| Clustering and graph rules | PAM, FURS, MaxCD | Rio et al. (2021); Tibbs-Cortes et al. (2022) |

## What the comparisons found

* CDmean was the best targeted criterion, and the lowest mean relationship the best untargeted one, in the benchmark of Fernández-González et al. (2023). A training set of 50-55% of the candidates (targeted) or 65-85% (untargeted) reached 95% of the maximum accuracy.
* CDmean and PEVmean beat clustering under strong population structure in oat (Rio et al., 2021), yet PEVmean was the weakest in a multi-parental wheat population (Zhang et al., 2021). No criterion wins everywhere.
* The goal matters. Criteria that maximize the mean accuracy are not the best for picking the top genotypes (Chen et al., 2024).
* We found no peer-reviewed deep-learning or active-learning method for choosing training individuals in genomic prediction. A recent review names it as a future direction (Alemu et al., 2024).

## A practical rule

1. Use a targeted search whenever the test set is genotyped.
2. Compare at least two criteria on your own data against random sets of the same size, as in [Getting started](getting-started.html).
3. Check the convergence of the search.
4. Use the training set size from `SSDFGS()` as the starting point, and expect to need more individuals for an untargeted design.
